title: Bedrock Whiteboard
subtitle: Claude on Bedrock, from silicon to a prompt in Sydney: the whole story first, then six chapters.

slides.title: The whole story in one picture
what: Trained outside your Region, on Trainium2, Google TPUs and NVIDIA GPUs. Sydney only runs inference
The checkpoint lands in a Bedrock-owned model deployment account in each Region. Anthropic can't access it
Your app calls bedrock-runtime.ap-southeast-2. Logs, metrics and the bill stay in your account
slides.say: AWS runs the model in your Region. For Opus, Sonnet and Haiku your prompts never go to Anthropic; Mythos-class models are the exception (C7a).

slides.title: Anatomy of one accelerator
what: One package: a compute die (cores + tens of MB of SRAM) ringed by HBM stacks on a TSMC CoWoS interposer
HBM moves TB/s to the die. Host DRAM sits behind PCIe (~64 GB/s each way), so weights and KV cache live in HBM
NVLink, NeuronLink and TPU ICI join packages so one model can span 8–64+ chips
slides.say: The memory is part of the chip. That's why HBM capacity decides how much model fits.

slides.title: NVIDIA vs Trainium vs Google TPU: memory per chip
what: NVIDIA: H100 80 GB → H200 141 GB → B200 192 GB → B300 288 GB, at up to 8 TB/s
Trainium2 96 GB / 2.9 TB/s → Trainium3 144 GB / 4.9 TB/s. TPU v5p 95 GB, Trillium 32 GB, Ironwood 192 GB / 7.4 TB/s
NVIDIA sells everywhere. Trainium is AWS-only, TPU is Google-Cloud-only. Claude runs on all three
slides.say: Three chip families, one pattern: more HBM and more bandwidth every generation.

slides.title: Who supplies the parts: market share
what: HBM, Q2 2026 (Counterpoint): SK hynix 50%, Samsung 33%, Micron 18%. SK hynix was 64% a year earlier
AI accelerators, 2026 estimates: NVIDIA ~75–85%, custom chips ~15–20% (TPU ~6–8%, Trainium ~2–3%), AMD ~5–7%
Every accelerator needs HBM, so HBM supply caps how fast anyone adds capacity
slides.say: Three companies make all the HBM. NVIDIA still sells most accelerators, but custom chips are growing.

slides.title: One rack, physically
what: GB200 NVL72: 18 compute trays (2 Grace CPUs + 4 Blackwell GPUs each), 9 NVLink switch trays, power shelves
72 GPUs, 13.4 TB HBM3e, 130 TB/s NVLink, ~120 kW, liquid-cooled, ~1.36 tonnes
AWS: Trn2 UltraServer 64 chips / 6 TiB. Trn3 UltraServer up to 144 chips / 20.7 TB. Rack power isn't published
slides.say: One AI rack draws what ten enterprise racks do, and it needs liquid cooling to survive it.

slides.title: "Memory-constrained" doesn't mean the context window
what: It means HBM, in three ways: bandwidth (decode re-reads it every token), capacity (weights + KV cache per chip), and supply (three makers)
The context window is a consequence of capacity: longer context means fewer users per chip
Micron says HBM is sold out for 2026. One bit of HBM costs ~3 bits of ordinary DRAM in fab capacity
slides.say: The chips aren't short of maths. They're short of fast memory, and the world has three suppliers.

slides.title: Compute stack: silicon to inference
what: Training is paid once per checkpoint, and again every model generation. RL post-training is a big repeated cost
Inference is the cost that grows with usage
Decode is limited by memory bandwidth, not compute (slide 7)
slides.say: Training is the entry ticket. Inference is the running bill, and it scales with your users.

slides.title: Trained on many clouds, served per platform
what: Fan-in (training) and fan-out (serving) are independent
Multi-cloud compute is a supply hedge, not a request path
A Bedrock call is served on AWS end to end, on Trainium and GPU
slides.say: Your request never hops to another cloud. Bedrock traffic stays on AWS.

slides.title: Where Claude is trained vs where it is served
what: Training: Project Rainier (over 1M Trainium2 chips, Indiana), up to 1M Google TPUs, and NVIDIA GPUs
Serving on Bedrock: Trainium2 and NVIDIA GPU instances. AWS doesn't publish which chip serves which model. Inferentia has no public link to Claude
HBM per chip: Trainium2 96 GB, H100 80 GB, H200 141 GB, B200 192 GB
slides.say: Training happens once, somewhere big. Your Region only runs inference.

slides.title: Serving one Region vs training the model
what: Inference: many independent replicas near users, across AZs, sized for peak. Fleet size isn't published
Pretraining: one synchronous job on one tightly coupled site. Project Rainier: ~500K Trainium2 at launch, 2.2 GW planned
RL post-training: generate rollouts, score them, update weights. Repeated for every model version
slides.say: Sydney runs replicas of a finished model. Building the model takes a gigawatt campus somewhere else.

slides.title: How the model lands in Sydney, Melbourne and Auckland
what: Each Region has one Bedrock-owned model deployment account per model provider
Opus, Sonnet, Haiku: prompts and outputs aren't stored or shared. Mythos-class models (e.g. Fable 5) need provider_data_share: 30 days kept by Anthropic
How weights are copied between Regions, replica counts and AZ placement aren't published
slides.say: The weights are a copy AWS operates. What you send stays with AWS, except on Mythos-class models.

slides.title: Inside one request: prefill, then decode
what: Prefill runs the whole prompt in parallel and writes the KV cache into HBM. It's compute bound
Decode makes one token per step and re-reads weights plus KV cache from HBM every time. It's memory-bandwidth bound
Large models are sharded across 8–64 chips over NVLink or NeuronLink
slides.say: The first token is a compute problem. Every token after that is a memory problem.

slides.title: Why memory, not compute, is the bottleneck
what: Each decoded token reads all active weights plus the KV cache from HBM, then does little math
Batching reuses each loaded byte across requests. Prefill is compute bound, decode memory bound
Longer context grows the KV cache. MoE cuts active params, not resident memory
slides.say: Generating text is a memory-bandwidth problem. That's why batching and long context drive cost.

slides.title: Prompt caching: where the cache actually lives
what: The cache is the prefix's KV tensors, kept in accelerator HBM after the request ends. It isn't in the compute cores
TTL is 5 minutes by default, or 1 hour. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 need at least 512 tokens per checkpoint
Writes cost 1.25× (5 min) or 2× (1 h) input. Reads cost 0.05× on Opus 5.5, 0.1× on most models. With CRIS, expect more cache writes
slides.say: Same prefix inside the TTL means you skip most of the work and pay a tenth.

slides.title: Sizing: chips, memory, power, money
what: Illustrative only: Claude's parameter count isn't published. This uses a made-up 400B model at FP8
8 × H200 = 1,128 GB HBM. 400 GB of weights leaves ~700 GB of KV cache, which is ~17 full 200K-token sessions
~10 kW per node and ~$46K a month on-demand (p5en, us-east-1), before redundancy
slides.say: You're not buying GPUs. You're buying a slice of a fleet AWS keeps full.

slides.title: The Claude lineup on Bedrock today
what: Opus 5.5 ($4/$20) and Sonnet 5.5 ($2/$10) shipped in Sep 2026, both with 1M context. Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5) is still the fastest
From Sydney: Opus 5.5 and Haiku 4.5 on au. + global.. Sonnet 5.5 on global. only at launch. Fable 5.1 on global.
New IDs have no date suffix: anthropic.claude-opus-5-5. Add au. or global. on runtime
slides.say: Pick the model by capability, price and where it can run from Sydney. Those three don't always line up.

slides.title: Two Bedrock endpoints for Claude
what: Sydney app on bedrock-runtime.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com calling au.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, which keeps processing in Australia
Runtime has the AWS extras: cross-Region inference, Guardrails, structured outputs, cost per team via app inference profiles
Mantle (bare ID anthropic.claude-opus-5-5) is for agent features: server-side tools, web search, async jobs. In-region only
slides.say: Pick the endpoint by the features you need. Price doesn't decide it.

slides.title: Which endpoint, which inference profile
what: In-region: strictest residency, lowest throughput
Geo (apac. au. jp. us. eu.): more throughput, processing stays in the geography
Global: most throughput at baseline price. Geo and in-region cost ~10% more (every model since Sonnet 4.5). Enforce with IAM on bedrock:InferenceProfileArn + SCP
slides.say: Residency vs. throughput is the dial. Global is cheapest and biggest. Geo keeps processing inside the geography.

slides.title: How customers consume it: APIs and the token meter
what: Runtime: InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, Converse, ConverseStream, CountTokens, plus Messages and Chat Completions
Mantle: Messages, Chat Completions and Responses, in-region only. Batch goes through the bedrock control plane
Quota counts input + 5 × output and reserves max_tokens. The bill counts real tokens, with cache reads at 5–10% of input
slides.say: Throttling is about the quota. Cost is about the bill. They're metered differently.

slides.title: How a runtime request burns TPM quota
what: max_tokens is reserved against quota when the request starts
Output tokens count 5× for Claude 3.7 and later
No RPM limit since May 2026. Runtime has one TPM per model; mantle splits input and output
slides.say: Throttling comes from the reservation, not the bill. Set max_tokens near what you actually expect.

slides.title: Tokens to dollars: a Sydney team of 1,000
what: 1,000 devs × 50 requests × (20K in + 1K out) = 1.0B input and 50M output tokens a day
Opus 5.5 on au.: ~$5,500 a day without caching, ~$2,270 with 80% cache reads (~$121K vs ~$50K a month)
Sonnet 5.5 is ~$2,500 a day uncached, but only on global. from Sydney at launch. Quota: ~2.6M TPM on average
slides.say: Caching cuts this bill by more than half. Picking the model is a residency decision as much as a price one.

slides.title: What moves with cross-Region inference
what: The model runs in a destination Region
Request and response still enter and leave through the source Region
CloudWatch, CloudTrail, invocation logs and price stay with the source Region
slides.say: Only the compute moves. Your logs, bill and entry point stay home.

slides.title: Data residency: what crosses the AU and NZ border
what: au. routes between Sydney, Melbourne and, since the NZ launch, Auckland. Confirm with aws bedrock get-inference-profile --inference-profile-identifier au.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5
Prompt and completion cross the border during processing. Logs, metrics and the bill stay in the source Region. On Mythos-class models (e.g. Fable 5), Anthropic also keeps them for 30 days
global. can go anywhere. Lock the choice down with an IAM condition on bedrock:InferenceProfileArn plus an SCP
slides.say: Pick the profile that matches your border, then make it impossible to pick another.

slides.title: "Claude on AWS": two products, one exception
what: Bedrock: AWS runs inference and is the data processor. Anthropic has zero operator access, and prompts aren't stored or shared
Exception: Mythos-class models on Bedrock (e.g. Fable 5) also send Anthropic a copy, kept 30 days (provider_data_share)
Claude Platform on AWS (Marketplace): Anthropic runs inference and is the data processor. AWS only handles billing and IAM. Inference geo is US or Global, with no AU option
slides.say: Paying through AWS isn't the same as AWS processing your data. Ask who runs the inference that sees the prompt.

slides.title: The sovereignty ladder: which rung does the customer need?
what: Rungs: data at rest → processing location → safety-retention location → in-country inference mandate → sovereign hosting
Rung 3 is live: Mythos-class models (e.g. Fable 5) on Bedrock require provider_data_share (30 days with Anthropic) since June 2026
Reported (Bloomberg, Aug 2026): option to keep that 30-day data in your own cloud by end of 2026. Not a published policy yet
slides.say: Most customers need rung 2, not rung 5. Find their rung before selling them sovereignty.

slides.title: Pool globally, or build in-country?
what: Economics favours one global pool: scarce chips go further, so global. is the cheapest profile
Politics favours local fleets: Australia's National AI Plan (DC capacity 1,350 → 3,100 MW by 2030), Korea's national AI centre, IndiaAI, NZ Kererū.ai
New capacity lands in three places: hyperscaler Regions, sovereign/neocloud operators, enterprise private AI
slides.say: Regulated and government workloads go in-country. Everyone else rides the global pool.

slides.eyebrow: 6 · Example: Claude Desktop on Bedrock · 1 of 6
slides.title: The whole flow on one whiteboard
what: IT configures the app, the user signs in with work SSO, the laptop talks straight to Bedrock in the customer's account
Five boxes and five numbered arrows. The next five slides walk them one at a time
No Anthropic login, no API keys, no Anthropic service in the request path
slides.say: Claude Desktop is just another AWS client. It signs in like any AWS app and calls Bedrock in your own account.

slides.eyebrow: 6 · Example: Claude Desktop on Bedrock · 2 of 6
slides.title: IT pushes the config
what: Jamf or Intune pushes managed settings: plist domain com.anthropic.claudefordesktop on Mac, HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Claude on Windows
Sets provider = Bedrock, Region, models, allowed folders and the SSO start URL
Policy is spread over several keys (allowedWorkspaceFolders, coworkEgressAllowedHosts, …). There's no single sandbox switch
slides.say: IT owns the setup. The user installs nothing extra and can't point the app at another provider.

slides.eyebrow: 6 · Example: Claude Desktop on Bedrock · 3 of 6
slides.title: User signs in with their work identity
what: The app opens the system browser for IAM Identity Center device sign-in
Identity Center is federated to Okta or Entra, so it's the corporate login and MFA
Signing in straight to the IdP only works behind your own auth proxy. Bedrock doesn't accept IdP tokens
slides.say: Same SSO, MFA and offboarding as every other AWS app they already use.

slides.eyebrow: 6 · Example: Claude Desktop on Bedrock · 4 of 6
slides.title: The app gets short-lived AWS credentials
what: Identity Center tokens sit in Keychain (Mac) or DPAPI (Windows)
Each session swaps them for permission-set role creds via portal.sso
Keys: inferenceBedrockSso{StartUrl,Region,AccountId,RoleName}. Set the permission-set session to 8–12 h
slides.say: No long-lived keys on the laptop. Disable the user in the IdP and access ends with the session.

slides.eyebrow: 6 · Example: Claude Desktop on Bedrock · 5 of 6
slides.title: Prompts go straight to Bedrock
what: The laptop calls Bedrock in the customer's account, SigV4-signed. Claude Code uses InvokeModelWithResponseStream
Models are inference profiles: global., us., eu., apac., jp., au.
Optional VPC endpoint or LLM gateway in front. Gotcha: no shell sandbox on Windows
slides.say: Your account, your Region, your network controls. Anthropic never sees the traffic.

slides.eyebrow: 6 · Example: Claude Desktop on Bedrock · 6 of 6
slides.title: Every call is tied to a real user
what: CloudTrail userIdentity = AWSReservedSSO_<PermSet>/<user>
CUR 2.0 IAM principal cost allocation adds line_item_iam_principal, so cost per user
A Bedrock API key is shared and breaks per-user attribution, so avoid it. OTel export also carries enduser.id
slides.say: Audit and chargeback come built in. Who called which model, and what it cost.

slides.title: Recap: the whole story in one picture
what: Hardware: accelerators live and die by HBM. Three companies make it, and it's sold out
Model: trained elsewhere at gigawatt scale, then copied into Bedrock accounts in each Region. Serving: prefill, decode, KV cache in HBM
Bedrock: pick model, endpoint and profile, then quota and bill follow. Data: pick the sovereignty rung the customer actually needs
slides.say: Silicon, model, serving, Bedrock, data rules, and one real deployment. That's the whole path from a chip to a prompt in Sydney.
